Les effets précis, les limitations et les conditions d'utilisation de ces Listes restent ceux prévus par les mécanismes effectivement disponibles dans MERP-RMU.

Le Magicien possède une forte orientation vers les compétences magiques et intellectuelles. Le Développement des Points de Puissance, la Manipulation de la Puissance, la Perception de la Puissance, les Connaissances magiques et les compétences de Lancement de Sorts occupent une place importante dans sa formation.

Les Sorts dirigés représentent une spécialisation essentielle pour les praticiens qui souhaitent employer efficacement les attaques élémentaires prévues par leurs Listes. Les compétences martiales ordinaires demeurent secondaires, même si certains personnages développent un entraînement adapté à leur culture ou à leur expérience personnelle.

Une distinction importante concerne le rapport entre le Magicien et les autres professions de l'Essence. L'Alchimiste consacre principalement ses connaissances à l'intégration de la magie dans les objets et les préparations matérielles, tandis que le Magicien intervient directement sur les forces élémentaires. Le Sorcier, qui associe l'Essence à la Théurgie dans l'adaptation MERP-RMU, appartient à une tradition magique différente.

Le Magicien doit également être distingué des Istari. Gandalf et Saruman possèdent une nature de Maiar et des missions particulières, dont la portée dépasse les capacités ordinaires des personnages. Leur apparence de vieillards savants et certaines manifestations de leurs pouvoirs peuvent inspirer le jeu, mais ils ne représentent pas directement la profession définie par RMU.

Il convient enfin de distinguer les grandes réalisations magiques décrites par Tolkien des effets accessibles à travers les Listes de sorts. Les œuvres de Fëanor, les enchantements des artisans d'Eregion et les pouvoirs des Valar appartiennent à des traditions et à des échelles de puissance différentes. Les six Listes élémentaires constituent la traduction ludique d'une forme particulière de magie, adaptée à la progression des personnages.

Dans MERP-RMU, l'existence des Magiciens demeure fortement liée à l'histoire et aux traditions des peuples. La disponibilité des enseignements peut dépendre de l'Âge, de la Culture, de la présence d'un maître ou de l'accès à des connaissances conservées dans des établissements spécialisés.

Enfin, les manifestations de l'Essence restent soumises aux règles de l'Ombre et de la Corruption propres au module. Les pouvoirs élémentaires ne sont pas intrinsèquement corrompus, mais certains usages, particulièrement lorsqu'ils servent la domination ou attirent l'attention de forces hostiles, peuvent entraîner les conséquences prévues par ces règles.

Le Magicien prend toute sa dimension lorsque ses connaissances et sa puissance contribuent aux choix de la compagnie, à la découverte des traditions anciennes et aux responsabilités qu'entraîne l'usage de forces capables de transformer profondément le monde matériel.

Magician

Essence and the Mastery of the Elements

For three days, autumn rains have swollen the rivers of Lebennin. The roads have become quagmires, ditches are overflowing, and several farms near the Serni have had to move their herds to higher ground. Downstream from a small village, the river has begun to wash away the earth supporting an ancient stone bridge. One of its arches still stands, but several feet of its foundations lie exposed, and every fresh rise in the water threatens to carry the crossing away.

In the morning, a man arrives from Pelargir, accompanied by a young servant leading a horse laden with chests and rolls of canvas. He wears a dark woollen cloak, a travelling tunic, and heavy boots whose leather has endured many days of rain. His hair is turning grey at the temples, and his hands, rather fine for a man who travels so frequently, bear small, old burns near the fingers.

The village headman takes him to the bridge. Several workmen have begun strengthening the bank with stones and logs, but the force of the current makes their labour dangerous. Part of the retaining wall collapsed during the night, and the wheel of the nearby mill has stopped beneath the branches swept down by the floodwaters.

The stranger examines the structure at length. He questions the miller about floods in previous years, measures the width of the scour beneath the foundations, and asks to see the stones that fell during the night. Then he unrolls a parchment upon a table sheltered beneath an awning and draws several lines with a graduated rule.

Before long, the nature of the problem becomes clear to him. The foundations rest upon a layer of compact earth, but the water has forced a passage between several stone blocks. If the current continues its work, it will eventually sweep away the material upon which the arch rests.

He asks the workmen to clear the bridge and prepare dressed stones beside the bank. Once everyone has withdrawn, he descends onto a narrow platform overlooking the water. For a few moments he stands motionless, watching the eddies. Then he raises one hand and slowly speaks several words in a language unknown to the villagers.

A few paces away, the current changes. Part of the water turns aside from the foot of the arch, exposing the loosened blocks and the earth they still hold in place. The man then fixes his attention upon the stones. A low rumble passes through the masonry, several fragments shift, and the gap threatening the foundations gradually begins to close.

The effort leaves the Magician visibly weary. He withdraws to the bank and asks for water. The workmen stare in astonishment at the newly accessible area, while their foreman examines the stones that have been set back in place. Much work remains, but they now have several hours in which to strengthen the structure before the river resumes its full force.

The Magician points out the elements that must be replaced and the places where new stones will distribute the loads more effectively. He has studied ancient buildings and knows enough of the mason's craft to understand the limits of what he has accomplished. The power he has employed has given them a chance to save the bridge; the future soundness of the structure will depend upon the quality of the repairs.

Late in the afternoon, the miller finds him near his dwelling. The man has opened one of his chests and is examining a collection of small instruments spread across a table. He is trying to understand why the waters attacked this part of the bridge rather than the other. A new drawing takes shape upon his parchment, accompanied by measurements that his assistant records as he dictates them.

The miller asks whether he could make the flood itself disappear. The Magician smiles, then explains that the river will continue to flow down from the hills for as long as the rains persist. There are ways to divert part of its course or alter its movement for a time, but the entire valley remains subject to the waters that gather within it.

Before taking his leave, the miller offers him a place beside the hearth for the night. He hopes the stranger will remain until the repairs are complete.

The Magician accepts. He has already noticed that several stones in the old structure bear the marks of a much earlier work, whose methods strike him as remarkable. He wishes to examine them before setting out again.

For nearly thirty years, this man has devoted his life to the study of the forces that act upon matter. Stone, water, air, fire, and light are the subjects of his research. He has learned to recognise their properties, to measure the consequences of their transformations, and to use Essence to act directly upon the physical world.

He is a Magician, and his art finds as many applications in the works that preserve communities as in the formidable displays of power remembered in tales of war.

The Hidden Forces of the World

Middle-earth has a history deeply bound to the forces of nature. Mountains were raised or broken during the ancient wars, seas swallowed entire lands, and forests retreated before fires, clearing, and upheavals of the world. The peoples who inhabit Arda know the power of these phenomena, whose consequences have shaped their territories since the earliest Ages.

The Magician devotes his studies to the properties of matter and the forces acting upon it. He seeks the principles that explain the movement of water, the transformations caused by heat, the reactions of metals, and the changes affecting air or light. His magic enables him to intervene directly in certain phenomena, employing Essence according to the teachings he has received.

This vocation demands a particular relationship with knowledge. Observation of the world is the first stage of his work. An unusual phenomenon, a substance whose properties remain unknown, or an ancient structure of remarkable design may inspire an investigation lasting many years.

The Magician learns to consider the consequences of his interventions. Changing the direction of a current may damage a bank farther downstream; moving a mass of stone may undermine the stability of a building. The heat that makes it possible to work metal becomes dangerous when it reaches flammable materials. True mastery therefore demands an understanding of the phenomena upon which magic acts.

Some Magicians devote their lives to study and teaching. They work in houses of learning, maintain collections of manuscripts, and pass on their knowledge to a few chosen pupils. Others travel the roads, seek the remains of ancient peoples, or place their powers at the service of a community.

The variety of their activities reflects the breadth of the profession. An experienced practitioner can assist with difficult construction, help travellers cross an obstacle, or protect a village threatened by a natural danger. In wartime, his powers also become formidable weapons, capable of profoundly changing the conditions of a confrontation.

Such power explains both the fascination and the suspicion that Magicians inspire. In regions where such manifestations remain exceptional, inhabitants interpret their presence according to local traditions. Some recognise an ancient knowledge worthy of respect; others fear the consequences of forces whose limits they do not understand.

Essence and the Magician's Art

The Magician's magic belongs to the realm of Essence, whose disciplines make it possible to act directly upon the structures and forces of the material world. His training rests upon an understanding of elemental phenomena and the means of directing magical power towards a particular effect.

This specialisation gives his art a particularly tangible character. The changes produced concern temperature, the movements of air, the flow of water, the consistency of certain substances, and manifestations of light and electricity. The effects available naturally depend upon the powers he has mastered, but the six elemental domains offer the practitioner considerable possibilities.

The study of Essence demands great intellectual discipline. Spells have conditions of use, limitations, and consequences that the Magician must come to understand precisely. Experience teaches him to recognise situations in which a modest intervention will achieve more than a spectacular display.

Knowledge of materials plays an important part in this mastery. A Magician familiar with the properties of stone and mortar will employ certain powers more effectively during building work. One who has studied currents and atmospheric phenomena will better understand the effects of intervening upon water or wind.

Magical disciplines complement this experience. The apprentice learns to perceive power, direct it, and maintain sufficient concentration to use his spells in difficult circumstances. The most complex teachings demand a mastery that he will acquire only after many years.

This training helps explain why accomplished Magicians remain relatively rare in Middle-earth. Their knowledge requires time, competent masters, and access to traditions, some of which have vanished during the wars. A pupil without regular instruction may spend years discovering principles that a learned community could have taught in a few seasons.

As his abilities develop, the Magician often chooses the fields to which he wishes to devote his research. Some favour fire and light; others study the transformations of earth and water. The most learned practitioners seek to understand the relationships between several elements so that they may employ their complementary properties.

The power of Essence nevertheless remains closely tied to the knowledge of the person who directs it. The choice of spell, the conditions in which it is used, and the risks of the intervention often determine whether an undertaking succeeds.

The Ancient Lore of Middle-earth

Tolkien's tales describe many manifestations of power capable of affecting the physical world. Some belong to the Valar and the Maiar, others to the arts of the Elves or the traditions of peoples whose knowledge surpasses that of ordinary Men.

In the earliest days of Arda, the Valar take part in shaping the world. Aulë possesses exceptional knowledge of matter and works fashioned by hand, while Ulmo holds dominion over the waters. Manwë is associated with the winds and the airs, and the ancient works of Varda give the lights of the heavens a particular significance.

These powers belong to the very nature of the Valar. The traditions of mortal Magicians are comparable to them neither in origin nor in scope. They nevertheless bear witness to the essential place held by the elements in the conception of the world.

The Elves also developed remarkable knowledge. Among the Noldor, the study of matter and the crafts of making attained a perfection to which the works preserved in Middle-earth still bear witness. Fëanor remains the most celebrated figure of this tradition, through the Silmarils, whose creation ranks among the greatest achievements of his people.

The craftsmen of Eregion, and Celebrimbor in particular, carried on some of this knowledge during the Second Age. Their work joined a profound understanding of materials to arts whose full nature Men could scarcely comprehend. The Rings of Power bear witness to this tradition, although their making belongs to a field very different from ordinary elemental manipulation.

In the Third Age, Gandalf repeatedly displays extraordinary mastery of fire and light. He sets pine-cones aflame to drive off the Wargs in the Misty Mountains, brings forth light in darkness, and employs his powers to protect his companions. Such manifestations offer natural inspiration to Magicians who specialise in the elements.

Gandalf, however, belongs to the Istari, sent to Middle-earth in human guise to fulfil a particular mission. His nature as a Maia fundamentally distinguishes him from mortal characters who learn the magic of Essence.

The lore of the Númenóreans provides another inheritance. Their architects, mariners, and craftsmen possessed remarkable mastery of many disciplines. After the Downfall, some of their knowledge was preserved in the realms founded by the Faithful, where ancient works continued to inspire later generations.

The Magician of MERP-RMU takes his place among this wealth of traditions. His Spell Lists express certain possibilities of elemental manipulation in game terms, without equating the great achievements of the Eldar or the powers of the Istari with the ordinary abilities of his profession.

The Years of Apprenticeship

The Magician's training generally begins under a master capable of passing on the knowledge needed to study Essence. Some pupils come from families of scholars; others discover their vocation following an encounter or an event that reveals their magical aptitude.

The early years are devoted to observation and intellectual disciplines. The apprentice studies measurements, numbers, and the elemental properties of materials. He learns to recognise the changes caused by heat, understand the movements of water, and distinguish substances by their characteristics.

Even the most modest exercises often take a great deal of time. The master asks his pupil to record variations of temperature in a workshop, follow changes in the level of a river, or observe the transformation of a substance exposed to fire. These tasks develop his powers of attention and provide the knowledge he will later need to understand the effects he seeks to produce through magic.

His apprenticeship also includes the study of languages and manuscripts. Ancient traditions are sometimes preserved in writings that are difficult to obtain or comprehend, and whose interpretation requires a thorough knowledge of the peoples who transmitted them. A text of Númenórean origin and a treatise written by a Noldorin master may employ very different terms to describe similar phenomena.

Mastery of Essence is introduced gradually. The pupil learns to perceive certain manifestations of power, then to focus his attention on increasingly precise effects. His first experiments usually involve small quantities of matter, under conditions where the risks remain limited.

His master teaches him the necessary precautions. A simple error in estimating a temperature or choosing a material can cause an accident. Magical effects become harder to control when they concern extensive surfaces, great masses, or phenomena capable of spreading beyond their intended bounds.

The study of Directed Spells forms a distinct part of his instruction. It requires learning to aim certain offensive manifestations with precision, for their power would be dangerous without appropriate training. Magicians who pursue this specialisation spend considerable time mastering distances, movement, and the conditions of combat.

The transmission of knowledge is accompanied, finally, by rules of conduct. Some masters insist upon caution and reserve their powers for necessary tasks. Others believe that difficulties allow a disciple to discover the extent of his abilities more quickly. These differences profoundly influence the personality and habits of the future Magician.

After several years, the pupil has acquired a training that allows him to continue his research with greater independence. He nevertheless knows the limits of what he has been taught and will often need to seek other masters or ancient works to deepen his understanding of particular disciplines.

The Six Elemental Laws

The Magician's powers are organised into six Base Spell Lists, devoted to the principal elemental forces. Each constitutes a separate field of study, although their applications frequently complement one another in the situations the character encounters.

Earth Law concerns the manipulation of soil, stone, and certain inorganic substances. It makes it possible to act upon mineral structures according to the effects of the spells employed. Building work, the search for passages, and the alteration of certain obstacles provide natural opportunities to use this discipline.

Fire Law teaches mastery over heat and flame. Some powers make it possible to heat materials or create effects useful in everyday life; others provide access to particularly dangerous elemental attacks. Practitioners who pursue this path must acquire a precise understanding of the consequences of fire for materials and living beings.

Ice Law concerns cold, the formation of ice, and transformations associated with low temperatures. It finds applications in northern regions, on mountain journeys, or wherever freezing can alter the condition of a surface. Its offensive manifestations are also formidable weapons.

Light Law enables the practitioner to produce and manipulate certain luminous phenomena, as well as electrical effects. Light offers valuable means of observation and travel, while electrical manifestations have applications of considerable power. This discipline demands close attention to the conditions in which spells are employed.

Water Law concerns the movement and manipulation of water and certain other liquids. Its applications may be of interest to travellers, mariners, and communities established near waterways. Knowledge of currents and the properties of liquids gives the Magician a better understanding of the possibilities offered by this List.

Finally, Wind Law acts upon air and certain atmospheric movements. It allows influence over phenomena whose consequences affect navigation, travel, and living conditions. Practitioners who study this path learn to recognise the movements of air and the risks involved in changing them.

These six disciplines form the heart of the profession. A Magician may concentrate his training on two or three elements, or seek a more balanced knowledge of them all. His choices depend upon his education, the resources available to him, and the responsibilities he wishes to undertake.

Stone, Water, and the Works of Men

Among the applications of Essence, those concerned with construction and the maintenance of great works hold a particular place. The peoples of Middle-earth have left behind roads, bridges, fortresses, and cities whose remains bear witness to a remarkable understanding of matter.

A Magician who studies earth and water can help explain some of the phenomena responsible for their deterioration. Seepage weakens foundations, movements of the ground cause cracks, and floods threaten crossings built near rivers. Appropriate powers sometimes offer ways to intervene when ordinary methods would demand much time or expose workers to considerable danger.

Yet such work requires an understanding of construction. Moving a stone in an ancient wall may change how the loads are distributed. Diverting a current may cause erosion farther downstream. The experienced Magician therefore learns to consult craftsmen whose knowledge complements his own.

Such cooperation can give rise to lasting relationships. A master mason of Gondor will appreciate interventions that make his work easier, while still insisting that foundations be examined with the same rigour as those of any ordinary structure. A Khazâd craftsman may recognise the value of a remarkable manipulation of stone without considering that magic removes the need to understand the material's properties.

Ruins also provide an especially rewarding field of research. The abandoned fortifications of Arnor, the works of the Númenóreans, and the remains of ancient cities make it possible to study techniques whose principles have sometimes been lost. A Magician may spend several weeks examining an old arch, measuring the blocks from which it was built, and seeking to understand the reasons for its exceptional strength.

Such work gradually deepens his understanding of matter. The character discovers that enduring works often rest upon the combination of exact knowledge and great patience. His powers then become additional instruments, used to extend the understanding gained from builders and craftsmen.

Fire, Ice, and Light

Manifestations of fire and light are among the most impressive forms of magic. In regions where inhabitants know little of practitioners of Essence, the appearance of a flame without fuel or of light amid darkness readily inspires wonder.

Yet these disciplines have many everyday applications. Heat can be used to work certain materials, prepare substances, or protect a group exposed to cold. Light produced in an underground passage makes it easier to examine a structure or seek a way forward. The control of ice can temporarily change the conditions of travel or allow certain obstacles to be crossed.

The importance of these powers depends greatly upon the regions traversed. In the northern mountains, a Magician faced with a long period of frost will find particular uses for the disciplines of cold and heat. In the cities of Gondor, the same knowledge may serve scholarly investigations or specialised work.

Their use nevertheless carries dangers. Fire spreads through woodland or among houses built from flammable materials. A frozen surface becomes slippery and may cause accidents. Certain electrical manifestations present considerable peril to anyone nearby.

The Magician therefore learns to judge the consequences of every intervention. The precision of a spell sometimes matters more than its power, especially when companions or inhabitants stand close to the area affected.

Light also occupies a particular place in the traditions of Middle-earth. The ancient tales attach great importance to the lights created or preserved by the Valar and the Eldar. The Magician's elemental powers belong to a different discipline, but some characters may be profoundly influenced by this heritage and give their luminous manifestations a meaning beyond their immediate usefulness.

Wind and Flowing Waters

Mariners, merchants, and travellers understand the importance of winds and currents. Ships making their way upstream along the Anduin must reckon with the river's flow, while vessels leaving Pelargir depend upon the conditions encountered along the coasts of Gondor.

A Magician specialising in the laws of water and wind possesses remarkable means of acting upon some of these phenomena. His powers allow him to influence the movement of the elements within the limitations of the spells employed. Their usefulness becomes evident when a vessel must negotiate a difficult passage or a group is exposed to dangerous weather.

The experience of mariners nevertheless remains indispensable. A favourable wind in one direction may make a manoeuvre more difficult elsewhere. Altering a current may produce consequences that an inexperienced traveller would never have anticipated. A practitioner working alongside a captain gradually learns to understand the demands of navigation and respect the knowledge of those who practise it every day.

In inland regions, the same disciplines find other applications. Valleys exposed to violent winds, dangerous fords, and waterways whose levels change rapidly all provide circumstances in which magic can offer valuable assistance.

These powers nevertheless serve as a reminder of the immensity of natural forces. Storms sweeping across the seas, floods caused by weeks of rain, and atmospheric movements affecting entire regions often exceed the abilities of an ordinary practitioner. Experience teaches him to use his resources at the moment when a limited intervention can achieve the best result.

The Weapons of Essence

Elemental magic possesses considerable offensive potential. The Magician's Lists include manifestations capable of producing bolts, elemental balls, and certain effects dangerous to the areas they strike.

This power gives the profession a particular place in combat. A trained Magician can act at a distance and employ phenomena against which ordinary protection does not always function as it does against physical weapons. Attacks of fire, cold, or electricity confront his adversaries with different dangers, whose effectiveness depends upon the spells and the circumstances.

Preparation remains essential. A swordsman instinctively judges the distance to his opponent and the way he moves. The Magician must acquire comparable mastery of his offensive powers, particularly when their use requires skill in Directed Spells.

The conditions of the terrain also influence his decisions. A confrontation in a dry forest does not carry the same risks as a battle upon a rain-soaked plain. A narrow passage may favour certain manifestations, but becomes especially dangerous when his companions stand close to the enemy.

The management of magical power represents another responsibility. The resources available to the Magician are limited, and exhausting them in combat may leave him without sufficient means to face a fresh danger. Experienced practitioners learn to reserve their most demanding powers for circumstances that justify their use.

Such caution is particularly important in Middle-earth. A spectacular manifestation sometimes reveals the Magician's presence to enemies whose proximity he had not suspected. Lightning and flames attract attention, while some adversaries possess their own knowledge of magical phenomena.

The character must therefore learn to choose between force and discretion. His powers can make a decisive contribution to the protection of his companions, but their effectiveness also depends upon how they fit into the group's decisions.

The Traditions of the Peoples

The Magician's place varies greatly among the cultures of Middle-earth.

Among the Noldor, knowledge of matter and the crafts of making belongs to a very ancient heritage. An Elven Magician may study the properties of the elements under masters whose experience far exceeds that of Men. His research belongs to a tradition in which knowledge, craftsmanship, and extraordinary arts maintain close relationships. He must, however, be distinguished from the great Elven craftsmen whose achievements belong to other forms of lore.

Among the Dúnedain of Gondor, the study of Essence may derive from traditions preserved within certain learned families or passed down by specialised masters. A practitioner established in Minas Tirith may devote his research to ancient texts, while a Magician of Pelargir may develop the disciplines of water and wind more extensively. The needs of garrisons, craftsmen, and travellers may also guide his work.

In the communities of the Northern Dúnedain, the most specialised forms of magical knowledge remain rare. A character from one of these families may have been taught by an isolated master or during a stay at a place of learning. The preservation of Arnor's ancient writings and continuing ties with the Elves provide particular reasons to pursue certain investigations.

In Umbar, the traditions of Númenor's descendants have followed a different history. Some families have retained ancient knowledge, sometimes directed towards more authoritarian or destructive ends. A Magician attached to an influential house may employ his talents in maritime ventures, the defence of installations, or rivalries among the powerful. His personal convictions will determine how he responds to the demands of his patrons.

The Men of the eastern and southern regions may likewise possess their own traditions of elemental study. Their teachings depend upon the languages, customs, and knowledge preserved by their communities. Some practitioners serve rulers; others live in more isolated settlements, where their lore is passed on to a handful of disciples.

In the rural regions of Rhovanion, the presence of a Magician is generally an exceptional occurrence. Inhabitants are more familiar with traditions associated with animals, plants, or practical knowledge. A practitioner of Essence may nevertheless exercise his art there, particularly if he was trained elsewhere or if his family preserves a rare teaching.

This diversity gives the character particular habits and responsibilities. An Elven scholar whose research extends over several centuries has a different relationship with his art from that of a young Gondorian taught by a demanding master. The traditions of Umbar, the lore preserved in the North, and practices transmitted among the peoples of the East offer other ways of understanding elemental power.

Cultural origin is therefore essential to understanding how the Magician learned his art, the limits he recognises in it, and the obligations that accompany its use.

Masters, Ancient Works, and Lost Knowledge

The transmission of elemental magic depends upon traditions that are sometimes fragile. The great upheavals of history have caused many scholarly communities to disappear, while wars have destroyed libraries and scattered the pupils of renowned masters.

A Magician wishing to deepen his knowledge must often seek out ancient works or practitioners capable of teaching particular disciplines. The archives of Gondor, Elven dwellings, and certain private collections offer precious resources, but access to them depends upon personal relationships and the trust placed in the researcher.

Studying a manuscript demands considerable labour. Its formulae may be written in an ancient language, accompanied by diagrams or references to phenomena whose explanation has been lost. Some pages describe experiments conducted under conditions difficult to reproduce, while others assume knowledge that the reader does not possess.

Cooperation between scholars then becomes particularly important. A Magician sometimes seeks the assistance of a linguist, craftsman, or historian able to illuminate part of his work. Such exchanges bring him into contact with circles far removed from his own profession and reveal the value of knowledge he might previously have regarded as secondary.

Rivalries are not absent from magical communities, however. A master may refuse to pass on teachings he considers dangerous, while a disciple aspires to surpass the limits imposed during his training. The discovery of an ancient work may cause conflict between those who wish to keep it secret and those who believe that sharing it would advance knowledge.

These tensions become more serious when the powers involved possess great destructive potential. A spell capable of disrupting a structure, producing intense heat, or altering an environment may be a precious resource, but also a threat in the hands of an imprudent practitioner.

Magical research thus places responsibilities upon the character that extend beyond his intellectual ambitions. His discoveries may benefit a community, transform his own understanding of the world, or draw the attention of those who wish to employ his knowledge for other ends.

Power and the Dangers of the Shadow

In Middle-earth, the pursuit of power has a history deeply marked by the works of Morgoth and Sauron. The servants of the Shadow learned to employ the forces of the world to build fortresses, forge weapons, and impose their dominion upon peoples.

The Magician who studies Essence must therefore consider the consequences of his discoveries. Knowledge intended to ease the work of craftsmen can be turned towards destruction. Powers capable of protecting a community become dangerous when used to impose a master's will or terrorise those who resist him.

Certain magical traditions are directly associated with the servants of Sauron. The Mouth of Sauron, a descendant of the Black Númenóreans, is described as having learned great sorceries in the service of the Dark Lord. His knowledge belongs, however, to a corrupted tradition whose nature must not be confused with the ordinary profession of Magician.

Temptation sometimes takes subtler forms. A researcher convinced that his work could protect his city forever may agree to pursue dangerous experiments. A practitioner eager to recover the lost knowledge of an ancient people may find himself drawn to writings of troubling origin.

The desire to command the elemental forces ever more completely is another source of danger. Early successes sometimes encourage excessive confidence, particularly among those whose training was rapid or whose powers earned the admiration of their contemporaries. A Magician accustomed to solving difficulties through power may gradually lose patience with solutions that require time and cooperation with others.

Overly conspicuous manifestations also carry particular risks. In regions watched by the servants of Sauron, spectacular magic may attract attention and betray the presence of a practitioner whose identity or intentions his enemies seek to discover.

The relationship with the Shadow nevertheless depends upon the character's choices. Mastery of Essence belongs to a discipline of knowledge; its use in the service of domination, cruelty, or corrupted practices engages the responsibility of the one who directs it.

This tension makes it possible to portray a Magician whose research carries genuine moral weight. His powers give him the capacity to act upon the physical world, but the manner in which he uses them determines the place he occupies among the peoples he encounters.

The Magician Through the Ages

The Magician's place depends profoundly upon the period chosen for the campaign.

In the First Age, the great traditions of the Eldar provide a particularly rich setting for studies of matter and natural forces. A Noldorin Magician may have trained under masters whose knowledge reaches back to the years spent in Aman. The realms of Beleriand possess craftsmen and scholars capable of transmitting remarkable lore, but the wars against Morgoth gradually bring about the destruction of many dwellings. Magical research thus takes place in a world where the ancient Powers still intervene directly in the fate of peoples.

In the Second Age, the presence of the Noldor in Eregion and the rise of Númenor offer new possibilities. Traditions of craftsmanship and scholarship meet, while Númenórean settlements encourage the study of building techniques, navigation, and the transformation of materials. A Magician may belong to a community of scholars, join expeditions, or seek knowledge preserved in the Elven realms. The growing influence of Sauron and the political changes in Númenor, however, make certain teachings particularly dangerous.

In the Third Age, the profession grows rarer, and its traditions are often scattered. In Gondor, some ancient knowledge survives in archives and among specialised masters. Among the Elves, the heirs of the great traditions continue to preserve lore that Men understand only imperfectly. In Umbar and certain eastern regions, other forms of magic may have been passed down within families or small communities. The advance of the Shadow demands particular caution from practitioners, especially when their powers produce visible manifestations.

In the Fourth Age, the fall of Sauron and the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom open new possibilities. Travel and exchange between regions become safer, and knowledge preserved through centuries of war may be brought together. A Magician can take part in rebuilding ancient works, studying rediscovered documents, or training new disciples. The gradual departure of the Elves also lends particular importance to preserving the lore they have passed on to the peoples of Middle-earth.

Each Age thus gives the profession a different significance. The Magician of the First Age belongs to a world in which great powers still shape the history of peoples directly; that of the Second Age shares in the flowering of knowledge among the Noldor and Númenóreans. In the Third Age, he often searches for fragments of an ancient inheritance, while his successor in the Fourth Age helps preserve and transmit the teachings that have survived the wars.

Leaving the Workshop and the Tower

The Magician's training often takes place in surroundings suited to study: a scholarly residence, a workshop equipped for experiments, or the chambers of a master surrounded by his disciples. Yet the knowledge he seeks frequently leads him beyond such places.

Some undertake a journey to recover a manuscript, examine the remains of an ancient structure, or meet a practitioner whose knowledge complements their own. An inscription discovered among ruins, a fragment of stone with unusual properties, or mention of a long-vanished school may justify an expedition lasting several months.

Others leave their master after a disagreement over the use of magic. A pupil believes that certain knowledge ought to be shared, while his mentor refuses to impart powers whose consequences he fears. A practitioner attached to a noble family may likewise choose exile rather than place his art at the service of an undertaking he condemns.

Sometimes the circumstances are more personal. An experiment has gone wrong and caused an accident; an ancient work has been stolen; a fellow pupil has disappeared during a dangerous investigation. The Magician then sets out upon a journey motivated as much by his responsibilities as by his desire to understand what happened.

Life on the road demands skills different from those acquired during years of study. Long marches, bad weather, and privation test a character accustomed to working in a controlled environment. His equipment must suit the conditions of travel, and his magical resources must be preserved for important circumstances.

Encounters with other professions gradually enrich his experience. A Ranger teaches him to recognise dangers in the terrain; a craftsman reveals the peculiarities of a material; an Alchemist shares knowledge of enchanted objects. Such exchanges allow the Magician to discover new applications for teachings he previously knew chiefly from manuscripts.

Within a company of adventurers, his powers find many uses. He helps overcome obstacles, alter certain conditions of the terrain, or protect his companions through elemental manifestations. His magical and scientific knowledge also becomes precious when the characters encounter ancient constructions or unusual phenomena.

The power of his spells does not remove his need to rely upon the experience of others. A warrior sometimes recognises a danger that no theoretical study would have enabled him to foresee, while a traveller accustomed to the wild lands discovers signs the Magician would never have noticed.

The relationships forged during adventure thus transform his understanding of his art. Knowledge gained from his companions, mistakes made, and hardships shared give new meaning to the teachings received during his training.

Playing a Magician

The Magician offers the opportunity to portray a character whose life is profoundly shaped by the pursuit of knowledge and mastery of the elemental forces. His cultural origin, apprenticeship, and the circumstances in which he discovered his powers nevertheless determine how he follows this vocation.

A young scholar of Gondor may have grown up in a family devoted to the learned traditions of Númenor before being entrusted to a master who possessed a few ancient works on Essence. A Noldorin Magician may be continuing investigations begun several centuries earlier, while a practitioner from Umbar has received demanding training in the service of an influential house. A traveller from the eastern peoples may possess teachings whose methods differ greatly from those known in the realms of the West.

The character's relationship with his master is an important part of his history. Was he trained by a respected scholar, or did he have to reconstruct part of his knowledge from incomplete manuscripts? Did an experiment long ago cause injuries whose traces he still bears? Is there an element that continues to elude his mastery despite all his efforts?

Years of study also shape his character. Some Magicians develop great patience, accustomed to repeating the same exercises until they achieve a satisfactory result. Others become especially demanding of their companions, particularly when those companions seem to act without considering the consequences of their decisions.

Success in certain experiments can also foster excessive confidence. A practitioner accustomed to employing his powers to solve material difficulties may sometimes underestimate the importance of human relationships or knowledge he does not possess. Conversely, a Magician who has suffered a serious accident may hesitate to use his abilities even when the circumstances would justify it.

His relationship with magical power deserves particular attention. One character may regard Essence as a discipline of knowledge demanding precision and restraint. Another may chiefly seek the means to protect those close to him or defeat the enemies threatening his people. Some wish to recover lost lore, while others aspire to surpass the achievements of their masters.

The profession is particularly well suited to campaigns centred on scholarly research, journeys, ancient ruins, and extraordinary phenomena. It also has a natural place in adventures where the characters must face dangers whose nature demands a profound understanding of the material world.

Over the course of his life, the Magician will discover that mastery of the elements does not necessarily grant him mastery over events or the beings around him. His knowledge will continue to grow, but the choices he makes, the relationships he maintains, and the responsibilities he accepts will give their true meaning to the powers at his command.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Magician in MERP-RMU

The Magician is a pure Essence spell user, specialising in the manipulation of the elemental forces of the material world.

His prime stats are Empathy (Em) and Reasoning (Re). Empathy is also the realm stat for Essence, while Reasoning represents the intellectual abilities required to study and understand complex magical disciplines.

He has six Base Spell Lists:

Spell ListDomain
Earth LawManipulation of earth, stone, and certain inorganic substances
Fire LawControl of fire and heat; offensive elemental manifestations
Ice LawCreation and manipulation of cold and ice
Light LawManipulation of light and certain electrical phenomena
Water LawControl of water and certain other liquids
Wind LawManipulation of air and certain atmospheric movements

The precise effects, limitations, and conditions of use of these Lists remain those established by the mechanics actually available in MERP-RMU.

The Magician has a strong orientation towards magical and intellectual skills. Power Point Development, Power Manipulation, Power Perception, Magical Lore, and Spellcasting skills hold an important place in his training.

Directed Spells represent an essential specialisation for practitioners who wish to make effective use of the elemental attacks provided by their Lists. Ordinary martial skills remain secondary, although some characters develop training suited to their culture or personal experience.

An important distinction concerns the relationship between the Magician and the other professions of Essence. The Alchemist primarily devotes his knowledge to embedding magic in objects and material preparations, while the Magician acts directly upon the elemental forces. The Sorcerer, who combines Essence with Channeling in the MERP-RMU adaptation, belongs to a different magical tradition.

The Magician must also be distinguished from the Istari. Gandalf and Saruman are Maiar by nature and have particular missions whose scope surpasses the ordinary abilities of characters. Their appearance as elderly scholars and certain manifestations of their powers may inspire play, but they do not directly represent the profession defined by RMU.

Finally, the great magical achievements described by Tolkien must be distinguished from effects accessible through Spell Lists. The works of Fëanor, the enchantments of the craftsmen of Eregion, and the powers of the Valar belong to different traditions and scales of power. The six elemental Lists are the game representation of one particular form of magic, adapted to character advancement.

In MERP-RMU, the existence of Magicians remains strongly tied to the history and traditions of the peoples. The availability of instruction may depend upon the Age, Culture, the presence of a master, or access to knowledge preserved in specialised institutions.

Finally, manifestations of Essence remain subject to the module's rules for Shadow and Corruption. Elemental powers are not intrinsically corrupted, but certain uses, particularly when they serve domination or draw the attention of hostile forces, may trigger the consequences provided for by those rules.

The Magician comes fully into his own when his knowledge and power contribute to the company's decisions, the discovery of ancient traditions, and the responsibilities involved in employing forces capable of profoundly transforming the material world.
